```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4)
library(bootqcc)
```

## 1. The problem

A Shewhart-type chart for a quantile (or any statistic) of a non-normal
distribution has no closed-form limits. `bootqcc` builds them by parametric
bootstrap (Efron 1979; Efron and Tibshirani 1993), in the spirit of
Padgett and Spurrier (1990) and Jones and Woodall (1998), for **any** family
that has `d`, `q` and `r` functions. Two situations must be distinguished.

* **Known parameters** (`bootqcc()`): the in-control parameters are given, and
  the chart is designed and its run length studied by simulation. This is the
  setting of most simulation studies in the literature.
* **Unknown parameters** (`bootqcc_phase1()`): only a Phase I sample is
  available. The parameters are estimated, and the estimation error makes the
  *actual* false-alarm rate random and, on average, larger than the nominal
  one (Quesenberry 1993; Jensen et al. 2006; Saleh et al. 2015).
  `bootqcc_phase1()` quantifies this effect and can correct it by a second
  bootstrap layer in the manner of Gandy and Kvaloy (2013).

## 2. Method in brief

For a subgroup $x_1,\dots,x_n$ let $\hat\theta$ be the maximum likelihood
estimate (Fisher 1922) and monitor $T=Q(u;\hat\theta)$, the estimated
$u$-quantile (any other function of $\hat\theta$ can be used). With the
parameters $\theta_0$ known, the limits are

$$
\mathrm{LCL}=\hat F_{T}^{-1}(\alpha/2),\qquad
\mathrm{UCL}=\hat F_{T}^{-1}(1-\alpha/2),
$$

where $\hat F_T$ is the empirical distribution of $T^*_b=T(\hat\theta^*_b)$,
$b=1,\dots,B$, and $\hat\theta^*_b$ is fitted to a sample of size $n$ drawn
from $F(\cdot;\theta_0)$. The limits are averaged over $M$ independent
repetitions. The run length is $\mathrm{RL}=\min\{t: T_t\notin[\mathrm{LCL},
\mathrm{UCL}]\}$; for fixed limits it is geometric with
$\mathrm{ARL}=1/p$, where $p$ is the probability that a subgroup signals
(Montgomery 2019). `bootqcc` estimates it by Monte Carlo.

With unknown parameters the limits are a function of the Phase I estimate
$\hat\theta$, so the false-alarm probability $p(\hat\theta)$ of the chart
*given* the Phase I sample is itself random. `bootqcc_phase1()` approximates
its distribution by an outer bootstrap: Phase I samples of the same size are
simulated from $F(\cdot;\hat\theta)$, the whole limit construction is repeated
on each, and $p$ is evaluated on a reference sample of in-control statistics.

## 3. Validation against exact results

For $X\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ the MLE of the rate is $1/\bar x$, hence
$T=-\log(1-u)\,\bar x$ with $\bar x\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(n,\,\text{scale}=1/n)$.
The exact control limits, the exact in-control ARL ($=1/\alpha$ for exact
limits) and the exact distribution of the conditional false-alarm probability
under estimation are therefore known, which gives a benchmark. The script
`inst/validation/exponential-validation.R` reproduces everything below.

```{r load-validation, include = FALSE}
f <- system.file("validation", "exponential-validation.rds", package = "bootqcc")
if (!nzchar(f)) f <- file.path("..", "inst", "validation", "exponential-validation.rds")
have <- file.exists(f)
if (have) val <- readRDS(f)
```

```{r partA, eval = have, echo = FALSE}
a <- val$partA
a$`B*alpha/2` <- a$B_alpha_2
knitr::kable(a[, c("alpha", "B", "B*alpha/2", "LCL", "LCL_exact", "UCL", "UCL_exact",
                   "ARL0", "ARL0_se", "ARL0_exact")], digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Known parameters: bootstrap limits and ARL0 (2000 runs) against the exact values. n = 5, u = 0.5.")
```

**Reading the table.** The bootstrap limits converge to the exact limits as
$B$ grows, and the in-control ARL converges to $1/\alpha$. When
$B\alpha/2$ is small (a handful of bootstrap points in each tail) the
empirical quantiles fall inside the true ones, the limits are too narrow and
the ARL is too small; this is a resolution effect of the empirical quantile,
not a bias of the method. A good rule is $B\ge 10/\alpha$, preferably
$B\ge 100/\alpha$; `bootqcc()` warns below the first threshold. The ARL
estimates carry Monte Carlo error (column `ARL0_se`), which is large for
$\alpha=0.0027$ because run lengths have a standard deviation close to their mean.

```{r partB, eval = have, echo = FALSE}
b <- val$partB
s <- b$summary
s$mean_FAP <- signif(s$mean_FAP, 3)
knitr::kable(s, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Limits", "Mean exact conditional false-alarm probability",
                "Share of Phase I samples with probability <= alpha"),
  caption = sprintf(paste("Unknown parameters: %d simulated Phase I samples (m = %d subgroups of size n = %d),",
                          "nominal alpha = %g. The false-alarm probabilities are computed exactly."),
                    b$S, b$m, b$n, b$alpha))
```

```{r partB2, eval = have, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Quantity = c("Mean false-alarm probability with the nominal level (exact)",
               "90% quantile of the false-alarm probability with the nominal level (exact)",
               "Level that makes the mean equal to alpha (exact)",
               "Same level estimated by the bootstrap (average over the samples)",
               "Level that makes the 90% quantile equal to alpha (exact)",
               "Same level estimated by the bootstrap (average over the samples)"),
  Value = signif(c(b$exact_mean_FAP_nominal, b$exact_q90_FAP_nominal, b$exact_alpha_mean,
                   b$est_alpha_mean, b$exact_alpha_quantile, b$est_alpha_quantile), 3)),
  caption = "Exact benchmark for the exponential case, and what the outer bootstrap recovers.")
```

The nominal $\alpha$ gives a mean false-alarm probability above $\alpha$, and
in a large share of Phase I samples the conditional probability exceeds
$\alpha$; the mean-adjusted level removes the average excess and the
quantile-adjusted level controls the share of unlucky Phase I samples.

*Comparison with other software.* The packages usually used for Shewhart
charts (for example `qcc` and `spc`) cover the normal and a few other
families, and none of them builds bootstrap limits for an arbitrary
distribution, so a like-for-like numerical comparison is not available for
the general case. The exact exponential results above are the benchmark used
here, and the limits for the normal mean obtained with `bootqcc` coincide in
the limit with the textbook $\mu\pm z\sigma/\sqrt n$ limits (see the check
below).

```{r normal-check}
set.seed(1)
fit_norm <- function(x) list(mean = mean(x), sd = sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2)))
mean_stat <- function(est) est$mean
ch <- suppressWarnings(bootqcc("norm", list(mean = 0, sd = 1), statistic = mean_stat,
                               n = 5, alpha = 0.0027, B = 20000, M = 5, arl_rep = 2,
                               fit_fn = fit_norm))
rbind(bootstrap = ch$limits, textbook = c(-1, 1) * qnorm(1 - 0.0027 / 2) / sqrt(5))
```

## 4. Case study: survival times (illustration)

We use the survival times (days) of the patients who died in the
`survival::lung` data (Loprinzi et al. 1994) to show the complete workflow
on real data. The data are not a manufacturing process, and the row order is
arbitrary, so the example demonstrates the mechanics of the method and is not
a claim that this process was in or out of control. Only deaths are used
(no censoring), and the first 100 observations in file order form the Phase I
sample, arranged as 20 subgroups of size 5.

```{r data}
library(survival)
x <- lung$time[lung$status == 2]
length(x)
phase1 <- matrix(x[1:100], ncol = 5, byrow = TRUE)
phase2 <- matrix(x[101:165], ncol = 5, byrow = TRUE)
```

A Weibull model is fitted with a fast profile-likelihood routine (the shape
solves a one-dimensional equation; Nelder-Mead on the log-likelihood would work
too but is slower):

```{r weibull-fit}
fit_weibull <- function(x) {
  lx <- log(x)
  g <- function(k) sum(x^k * lx) / sum(x^k) - 1 / k - mean(lx)
  k <- tryCatch(uniroot(g, c(0.05, 50))$root, error = function(e) NA_real_)
  if (is.na(k)) return(NULL)
  list(shape = k, scale = mean(x^k)^(1 / k))
}
fit_weibull(as.numeric(phase1))
```

A quick check of the Weibull fit by comparing the empirical and fitted
quantiles of the Phase I data:

```{r qq, fig.height = 4}
est <- fit_weibull(as.numeric(phase1))
p <- ppoints(100)
plot(qweibull(p, est$shape, est$scale), sort(as.numeric(phase1)),
     xlab = "Weibull quantiles", ylab = "Observed quantiles", pch = 19, cex = .6)
abline(0, 1, col = "red")
```

The chart monitors the median ($u=0.5$). With only 100 Phase I observations
the estimation error matters, so we use `bootqcc_phase1()`; $\alpha=0.01$
keeps the example fast (use $\alpha=0.0027$ and larger $B$ for a final design).

```{r phase1}
ch <- bootqcc_phase1(phase1, "weibull", u = 0.5, alpha = 0.01, fit_fn = fit_weibull,
                     B = 2000, R = 100, N_ref = 10000, adjust = "mean", seed = 123)
ch
```

The Phase II subgroups are then compared with the limits:

```{r phase2}
mon <- bootqcc_monitor(ch, phase2)
mon
plot(mon)
```

```{r fap-hist, fig.height = 3.6}
hist(ch$fap, breaks = 20, col = "grey85", border = "white",
     main = "Conditional false-alarm probability (nominal level)",
     xlab = "probability that a subgroup signals")
abline(v = ch$alpha, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
```

The histogram shows how much the false-alarm rate varies with the Phase I
sample alone when the nominal level is used; the red line is the target.

## References

Efron, B. (1979). Bootstrap methods: another look at the jackknife. *The
Annals of Statistics*, 7(1), 1-26.

Efron, B. and Tibshirani, R. J. (1993). *An Introduction to the Bootstrap*.
Chapman and Hall, New York.

Fisher, R. A. (1922). On the mathematical foundations of theoretical
statistics. *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A*, 222, 309-368.

Gandy, A. and Kvaloy, J. T. (2013). Guaranteed conditional performance of
control charts via bootstrap methods. *Scandinavian Journal of Statistics*,
40(4), 647-668.

Jensen, W. A., Jones-Farmer, L. A., Champ, C. W. and Woodall, W. H. (2006).
Effects of parameter estimation on control chart properties: a literature
review. *Journal of Quality Technology*, 38(4), 349-364.

Jones, L. A. and Woodall, W. H. (1998). The performance of bootstrap control
charts. *Journal of Quality Technology*, 30(4), 362-375.

Loprinzi, C. L., Laurie, J. A., Wieand, H. S., et al. (1994). Prospective
evaluation of prognostic variables from patient-completed questionnaires.
*Journal of Clinical Oncology*, 12(3), 601-607.

Montgomery, D. C. (2019). *Introduction to Statistical Quality Control*, 8th
edition. Wiley, Hoboken, NJ.

Padgett, W. J. and Spurrier, J. D. (1990). Shewhart-type charts for
percentiles of strength distributions. *Journal of Quality Technology*, 22(4),
283-288.

Quesenberry, C. P. (1993). The effect of sample size on estimated limits for
X-bar and X control charts. *Journal of Quality Technology*, 25(4), 237-247.

Saleh, N. A., Mahmoud, M. A., Keefe, M. J. and Woodall, W. H. (2015). The
difficulty in designing Shewhart X-bar and X control charts with estimated
parameters. *Computational Statistics and Data Analysis*, 87, 1-16.
